1:
Ellicott sets the whole chapter under one heading: the slow but certain working of divine retribution. Gideon's two faults at the end were his polygamy and his tampering with unauthorised worship, and the punishment for both falls on his house through the Canaanite kinsmen of his base-born son — in whom Ellicott traces the father's courage overshadowed by the mother's stock. Gill notes that the son had been reared at Ophrah though his mother lived at Shechem, so that this was a visit to his uncles; Clarke says its object was to have him proclaimed governor in his father's room. Henry supplies the motive: his mother had instilled ambitious thoughts, and the name his father gave him carried royalty in it. He had no call from God as Gideon had, and the proposal came from nobody but himself — none would have dreamed of making such a man king, Henry remarks, if he had not dreamed of it himself.

Henry observes that no son of Gideon had the least intention of reigning, all being of their father's mind that the Lord should rule; but those who design ill suspect others of it. Clarke sees the force of the question all the same — seventy tyrants or one? — and adds that a usurper must support his rule by whatever means come to hand. Ellicott calls the suggestion a calumny, since Gideon had expressly repudiated such rule. The word rendered men of Shechem is properly lords, a title that looks Canaanite rather than Hebrew; the town held a mixed population in armed neutrality, the Israelites having the upper hand but being fewer, much as the Normans among the English. His plea of bone and flesh was addressed to both halves of it, to the Ephraimites by birthplace and the Canaanites by blood — like that, Ellicott says, of the first Norman king born of a Saxon mother.

Keil and Delitzsch identify the treasury of the shrine dedicated to the covenant Baal, noting how often temple treasures were turned to political uses; Ellicott adds that an ancient temple served at once as sanctuary, fortress and bank, the hoard at Delphi having financed a sacred war. Gill cannot settle the value, shekels seeming too little to raise an army and talents too much for such a city, and suspects the number was chosen to match that of Gideon's sons. Henry draws the moral: a man who instead of punishing idolatry made himself thus early a pensioner to an idol was unlikely ever to defend Israel. With it he hired what Henry calls the scum of the country, men of broken fortunes and profligate lives — like leader like followers — and Clarke worthless men with nothing to lose, by the cunning management of whom most revolutions have been brought about.

Ellicott marks the massacre as the first mention in Scripture of the practice, common afterwards among Eastern despots, of forestalling conspiracy by destroying all one's brothers — a precedent followed by Baasha, Zimri, Jehu and Athaliah. Keil and Delitzsch hear an omen in the one stone: a formal execution, and a bloody prefiguring of the northern kingdom afterwards founded at this same Shechem, where each dynasty exterminated the last. Henry sees what ambition makes of a man, and what peril attaches to high birth, since it was their being sons of so great a father that exposed them — the lower, he concludes, the safer. Henry notes that God was not consulted whether they should have a king at all; that the Shechemites both abetted the murder and rewarded it with a diadem; and that the rest of Israel never stirred to avenge Gideon's sons. Ellicott ends on the place chosen — the terebinth where Joshua had set up his stone of witness, so that the neighbourhood of that very pledge of faithfulness lent the act its audacity.
7:
Henry marks this as the only testimony borne against the confederacy, and takes it for a sign that God had departed from the people that neither prophet nor judgment was sent. Jotham raised no army and set up no claim of his own — itself the answer to Abimelech's slander. Keil and Delitzsch describe Gerizim rising as a steep wall of rock some eight hundred feet above the valley; Ellicott doubts the actual summit and prefers a crag above the town, adding that the chanting delivery Orientals use carries astonishingly far in that air. Clarke supports this from a traveller in southern India who heard men converse from hill to hill without shouting. Ellicott also asks how Jotham dared risk it, and answers that a hillside full of caves gave him a start, that he may have had partisans, and that the pathos of his opening may have won a hearing.

Gill calls it the most ancient of its kind, framed seven hundred years before Aesop and exceeding anything of his; Clarke calls it the oldest and best in the world; Ellicott observes that this chapter gives us the first Israelite king, the first massacre of brethren and the first fable together, and that Scripture contains only one other. Keil and Delitzsch treat the parable as genuinely prophetic; Gill notes that no tree is named before the bramble but a fruitful one.

Henry reads the refusals as a compliment to Gideon and the judges before him, and as showing that wise men prefer being useful to being great. There was no occasion for the trees to want a king at all, since they are all the trees of the Lord which he has planted; and when they did, they applied not to the stately cedar but to the fruit-bearers. Each gave the same reason: office involves toil and care, costs a man his private advantages, and endangers his fruitfulness, since preferment makes men proud and slothful — which is why those who desire to do good are afraid of being too great. On the clause about honouring God and man, Clarke would render it gods, holding the parable accommodated to Shechemite idolatry, while Ellicott allows that gods and men may honour these things in the olive, referring it either way to the use of oil in sacrifice.

Henry calls the bramble a worthless plant not numbered among the trees, beginning with the curse and ending in the fire, and notes that this election alone was unanimous. It takes no time to consider but hectors at once, inviting them to trust in its shadow — a goodly shadow, Henry says, and how unlike the shadow of a great rock in a weary land — when they were likelier to be scratched by coming near; and it threatens fire against the cedars, being itself the likeliest of all things to be consumed. Clarke calls the promise the vain boast of a would-be sovereign, all promise and no performance, and the threat a strong figure, since the smallest fire reduces a bramble to ashes. Ellicott identifies the plant as the buckthorn and notes that the trees address it in a blunt imperative where they had been ceremonious with the others. Henry then has Jotham plead a father who fought their battles at the hazard of his life, and contrast the many sons who honoured Gideon's name and were murdered with the one who blemished it and was crowned. He leaves the issue to providence: if they prospered, they might say they had done well; if not, Abimelech and Shechem would be a plague and a ruin to each other. Ellicott marks the ironic echo of the bramble's own phrase in the supposition, and calls the son of his maidservant intentionally contemptuous, though the woman was no slave.
22:
Keil and Delitzsch note that the verb is not the ordinary word for reigning but one meaning to govern, chosen because this was no monarchy but a despotism, and that Israel means only the part of the nation which acknowledged him. Gill thinks it amazing that the people acquiesced instead of rising to avenge Gideon's sons, and remarks that the reign was short, as those of wicked princes often are. Henry says it is not recorded that he judged Israel or did his country any service; he held the title three years, and the triumphing of the wicked is short.

The evil spirit divides them. Keil and Delitzsch insist on a real demon rather than a mere temper, a power under Satan's influence though not Satan himself, and note that Elohim is used because divine justice is in view. Ellicott is more cautious: the word sometimes denotes an evil being and sometimes only an evil disposition. Clarke keeps it at the level of providence — God permitted jealousies which bred factions, and factions insurrections and slaughter. Henry takes both together: God allowed the great mischief-maker to sow discord, and their own lusts were themselves evil spirits; when a man's sin is made his punishment, God is not its author though the punishment is from him. Both he and Ellicott stress the ground of the quarrel, the blood of Gideon's sons laid on the men who shed it; Henry draws from it that God makes inquisition for innocent blood, that accessories are reckoned with as well as principals, and that confederates in wickedness are justly dashed one against another, blood being no lasting cement.

Clarke observes that God punished this bad man by the very persons who had raised him, often making the instruments of men's sins the means of their punishment, and places the ambush on the road between Shechem and Ophrah. Ellicott adds that the phrase need not mean they meant to seize him, and that disaffection in Palestine has always shown itself in a rise of brigandage. Henry sees the double effect: they would have made him their prisoner whom they had lately made their prince, and the robbing of travellers made the people uneasier when they saw he could not protect them.

Then Gaal arrives, and nobody knows who he was. Keil and Delitzsch take him for a knight-errant heading a company of freebooters, welcomed because the disaffected hoped he would serve their turn. Ellicott agrees and thinks him a Canaanite, his brethren forming the nucleus of a marauding band, and suspects the name as we have it is a contemptuous distortion. Henry notices the symmetry: Abimelech was the son of a servant by his mother's side and Gaal by his father's, so that one bramble contested with another. At the vintage feast the quarrel comes into the open. Keil and Delitzsch identify the offerings as the praise-offerings of a fourth-year vintage, eaten in the temple of the covenant Baal, the cursing coming when the men were heated with wine; Ellicott calls it a heathen analogue of the Feast of Ingathering and would render the verb abused. Henry presses the irony hardest: the very temple from which they had fetched the money to set Abimelech up was now the room they met in to curse him — how should Satan cast out Satan?

Ellicott compares Gaal's opening sneer to Nabal's about David, finds the next clause genuinely obscure, and explains the taunt about Jerubbaal: a son so descended is connected with neither Ephraimites nor Canaanites, and the Baal-fighter's son has no claim on Baal-worshippers. Clarke calls the wish that the people were under his hand the language of a sly demagogue, who sent his challenge only when he found his party strong. Henry judges that Gaal aimed not at recovering Shechem's liberty but only at changing its tyrant, turbulent spirits despising dominion and speaking evil of dignities.
30:
Gill notes that Abimelech had set Zebul over the city; Ellicott that the title suggests a military commandant. Henry observes that his anger was the hotter because Gaal had spoken slightingly of him, and guesses a little flattery might have bought him. Betrayers, he says, are often betrayed by their own, and the cursing of a king is strangely carried by a bird of the air; and asks how Shechem could hope to prosper with its own ruler in the enemy's interest. The adverb describing the message is disputed. Keil and Delitzsch report that it may mean with deceit or may be a misspelt place-name; Ellicott says the word occurs nowhere else and the versions differ, but that the message was plainly secret, Zebul dissembling until strong enough to throw off the mask; Gill gives both readings. Clarke reads the report that they fortify the city as meaning that under pretence of repairing the walls they were putting it in a state of defence; Ellicott would render it rather that they tyrannise over it.

Ellicott explains that the ambush was to catch the Shechemites finishing their vintage under Gaal's protection, and Keil and Delitzsch note the four companies laid in wait. At the gate — the usual station of rulers, though Ellicott thinks Gaal went there only to keep a look-out, and Clarke supposes he had some intimation of it — Gaal sees men coming down; Zebul answers that he mistakes the shadow of the mountains for men. Ellicott points out that the shadow would be advancing as the sun rose, and that Zebul speaks as though Gaal were still intoxicated from his feast; he confesses that Zebul's position is anomalous and the narrative too brief to explain it. Henry finds two purposes in it: to ridicule a man ready to fight a shadow, and to hold him in talk while the forces came up.

The place-names in Gaal's second sighting are obscure. Keil and Delitzsch give them as the navel of the land, the highest point of the surrounding country, and the wizard's terebinths; Ellicott takes the navel for a swelling hill, notes how it perplexed the versions, and would render the second the Enchanters' Terebinth. Clarke reports the alternatives — the way of the oaks, or of the magicians — supposing it a place where augurs lived.

Zebul then drops the mask. Keil and Delitzsch have him declare openly against Gaal and reproach his foolhardy speech; Henry hears an upbraiding — where is now that mouth of thine? — and remarks that proud people are often made to change their note and dread those they most despised, Gaal being challenged in the very terms he had used. Ellicott grants that this is the usual reading but offers another: unless Zebul was already secured against Gaal's vengeance, the words may be less a taunt than an expostulation against his rashness.

Keil and Delitzsch deny that Gaal went out at the head of the citizens, since only his own retinue was with him, and take the phrase to mean he fought while the lords looked on; Ellicott insists that he led them. Henry has him disheartened by Zebul's hectoring and finding his interest weaker than he supposed, so that he marched out and was quickly put to the worst — the loss falling on the townsmen, as it does in popular tumults, where the multitude are drawn into snares by men who promise glorious success. Ellicott calls it a complete victory, though Gaal got his men back inside at heavy cost. Abimelech, as Gill and Keil and Delitzsch note, did not force an entry but withdrew to Arumah, and Zebul used the interval to expel Gaal and his brethren; Ellicott passes on Josephus's account that he did it by accusing Gaal of cowardice, and observes that Gaal escaped by that expulsion the fate which shortly overtook Shechem.
42:
Keil and Delitzsch read the next morning's movement as innocent: the people went into the field not to make war but to work, perhaps to finish the vintage, and on that intelligence Abimelech laid three companies in ambush. Ellicott says no reason can be given why there were three this time rather than four, and draws the obvious inference about the man — those he cut down were husbandmen, not an armed host, and only a ruthlessly vindictive temper would have done it. Keil and Delitzsch have Abimelech's own division take station at the gate to cut off the retreat while the other two ran upon the people in the open; Ellicott notes that this time he intercepted them before they could get back, and had kept the post of honour and danger for himself. Gill observes that the men with him were his forces from Arumah, and that the word for his company may mean the heads, great men being among them.

The sowing of the ruined city with salt is the detail that draws comment, since it occurs nowhere else. Keil and Delitzsch take it for a symbolic act declaring that the place was to become a barren salt desert for ever. Clarke rejects that: the salt was not meant to make the ground sterile, since nobody would cultivate a city, but rather, salt being an emblem of incorruption, to perpetuate the memorial of the deed and to signify that the desolation was meant to be everlasting; he notes the custom in other nations, citing the razing of Milan. Ellicott sides with the harsher sense — the act devoted the city to barrenness — and observes that nothing could better show Abimelech's execration against the very populace to whom he owed his elevation; he cites both Milan and the salting of Coligny's house by royal command.

The survivors make for the temple. Gill infers from their being said only to have heard the news that the tower stood outside the city though near it, and identifies it with the house of Millo, so that this part of Jotham's curse was now accomplished. Keil and Delitzsch agree, and are careful about the motive: they went into the stronghold of the temple of the covenant god not to defend it but to seek sanctuary, having probably dealt treacherously with Abimelech themselves. Clarke takes the hold to mean the precincts of the temple, since a thousand men and women were gathered there together. Ellicott calls them the garrison of the house of Millo and canvasses the versions on the word for hold.

Then comes the fire. Gill describes Zalmon as a mountain near Shechem named from the shade of its trees, Ellicott as the nearest place where wood could be had for so hideous a design, adding that the name means shady and that the text speaks not of one axe but of axes. Keil and Delitzsch narrate the rest plainly: Abimelech cut a bough, laid it on his shoulder, told his men to do as they had seen him do, and they piled the branches on the hold and fired it over those inside, so that about a thousand men and women died. Gill pictures the column climbing back with the boughs on their shoulders, so that they looked like men that were trees walking; Ellicott recalls the scene in Macbeth where every soldier is bidden hew himself a bough. Ellicott marks the fulfilment: the words of Jotham had proved prophetic, and he compares the death of Zimri, burnt in the palace at Tirzah.
50:
Thebez is placed by Keil and Delitzsch thirteen miles from Shechem on the road to Scythopolis, surviving in a village of similar name; Gill reports the same distance from Jerome, adds a traveller's account of ruins and marble near Jacob's well, and notes that the town had rebelled; Ellicott takes it for one of the cities in the league of the covenant Baal. Henry supposes it a small place dependent on Shechem, and thinks Abimelech expected to repeat there what he had just done at the temple stronghold — not considering that an idol-temple's tower lay more exposed to divine vengeance than any other. Men who succeed in one desperate attempt, Henry remarks, think another not desperate. Ellicott notes how the constant mention of towers through these chapters betrays a disturbed country, not unlike England under King Stephen.

Ellicott concedes that Abimelech did not lack physical courage and had all his father's impetuous energy; Henry observes that the peril of coming near a besieged wall was cited long afterwards as a standing warning, but that God infatuates those he means to ruin. The stone is described with care. Gill and Ellicott identify it as a piece of the upper millstone, the runner whirled over the fixed stone beneath; Clarke notes that the phrase has also been taken for a piece of a chariot wheel though the versions understand a millstone, complains that the old English rendering of the verb is nonsense for a plain statement that she fractured his skull, and recalls Plutarch on Pyrrhus killed by a tile thrown by a woman. Ellicott explains the same crux as a printer's error for an intensive form.

The dying order to the armour-bearer is a point of honour. Clarke observes that it was a disgrace to be killed by a woman, quoting Seneca's lament over the death of Hercules, and suggests that Abimelech also feared what his enemies might do to him alive. Ellicott adds that the shift did not save him from the taunt, and notes how sensitive the ancients were about the manner of their death — the feeling that made Deborah exult over Sisera.

Henry gathers three circumstances of the death and finds a judgment in each: that he was killed with a stone, as he had killed his brethren upon one stone; that his skull was broken, vengeance aiming at the head that had worn the usurped crown; and that the stone came from a woman's hand, which he saw and knew, where Sisera died in ignorance. He draws the wider moral from the smallness of the place: having conquered the greater city, Abimelech made no doubt of the less and laid his bones by it — so are the mighty things of the world often confounded by the weakest. He had some colour for chastising Shechem, but when nothing would serve but that Thebez must be sacrificed to his rage as well, he was not merely disappointed but destroyed. Ellicott records that the army broke up at once, as ancient armies did on a leader's death, and quotes the judgment that with Abimelech expired this first abortive attempt at monarchy, the true King of Israel being still far off.

Gill notes that the wickedness rendered was done against Gideon's own family, and that the evil of the Shechemites lay both in helping to kill the brethren and in crowning the murderer. Keil and Delitzsch set the two verses of retribution side by side, and Clarke sums it up: both the fratricide and the unprincipled men who backed him had their iniquity visited on them, and though man's judgment may be avoided there is no escaping God's. He then returns to the fable, comparing it with the Sanskrit collection known in Europe as the fables of Pilpay, which a great orientalist of his day judged the most beautiful if not the most ancient in existence.
